references.text: The Israelites complained to Moses at the Red Sea and asked if there were no graves in Egypt, expressing that they would rather serve Egyptians than die in the wilderness. This shows the same pattern of complaining and desire to return to Egypt.
The people complained again to Moses because of thirst and accused him of bringing them out of Egypt to kill them. The same pattern of accusation against Moses and God is repeated.
The Israelites longed for the meat, fish, cucumbers, and melons they ate in Egypt. This reflects the same longing back to Egypt's food as in Exodus 16:3.
The people grumbled against Moses and Aaron and wished they had died in Egypt. They wanted to choose a leader to return to Egypt, the same attitude expressed in Exodus 16:3.
At Meribah, the people quarreled with Moses and said they wished they had died. They complained that they were brought out of Egypt to a place without grain, figs, or water.
The people spoke against God and Moses and asked why they were brought out of Egypt to die in the wilderness, complaining about the lack of bread and water.
The psalm describes how the Israelites were seized by desire in the wilderness and tested God in the desert. This summarizes the story of complaint from the wilderness journey.
Paul warns against grumbling as some of the Israelites did and were killed by the destroyer. He uses the wilderness journey story as a warning for believers.
The direct parallel where the people wish they had died in Egypt instead of facing the challenges of the wilderness.
Reference to the people's earlier complaint that they were better off in Egypt and their craving for meat.
The same theological pattern where the people prefer slavery in Egypt over the uncertainty of the wilderness.
The direct accusation that God brought them out to let them die in the wilderness.
The theological distortion where the people believe God brought them out of hatred to destroy them.
